text: Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Confine yourself to the present.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: We suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
author: Seneca

text: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a great deal of it.
author: Seneca

text: Begin at once to live, and count each separate day as a separate life.
author: Seneca

text: Sometimes even to live is an act of courage.
author: Seneca

text: No man is free who is not master of himself.
author: Epictetus

text: First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do.
author: Epictetus

text: A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.
author: Lao Tzu

text: Knowing others is intelligence; knowing yourself is true wisdom.
author: Lao Tzu

text: The best fighter is never angry.
author: Lao Tzu

text: Real knowledge is to know the extent of one's ignorance.
author: Confucius

text: Man is condemned to be free; because once thrown into the world, he is responsible for everything he does.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: Freedom is what you do with what's been done to you.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: We are our choices.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: Life has no meaning a priori. It is up to you to give it a meaning.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: In the depth of winter, I finally learned that within me there lay an invincible summer.
author: Albert Camus

text: Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: What does not kill me makes me stronger.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §8

text: He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows §12

text: You must have chaos within you to give birth to a dancing star.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: He who would learn to fly one day must first learn to stand and walk and run and climb and dance.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: Opinion is the medium between knowledge and ignorance.
author: Plato

text: The heaviest penalty for declining to rule is to be ruled by someone inferior to yourself.
author: Plato

text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
author: Socrates

text: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Go confidently in the direction of your dreams.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Simplify, simplify.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Not until we are lost do we begin to understand ourselves.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: What you do speaks so loudly that I cannot hear what you say.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: The only way to have a friend is to be one.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: To be great is to be misunderstood.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Act as if what you do makes a difference. It does.
author: William James

text: The problem of the world is that fools and fanatics are always so certain of themselves, but wiser people so full of doubts.
author: Bertrand Russell

text: Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not.
author: Epicurus

text: I think, therefore I am.
author: René Descartes

text: Experience without theory is blind, but theory without experience is mere intellectual play.
author: Immanuel Kant

text: Act only according to that maxim by which you can also will that it would become a universal law.
author: Immanuel Kant
source: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 4:421

text: Desire is the essence of man.
author: Baruch Spinoza

text: What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence.
author: Ludwig Wittgenstein

text: Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
author: George Santayana

text: The supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without fighting.
author: Sun Tzu

text: When we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.
author: Viktor Frankl

text: Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms — to choose one's attitude.
author: Viktor Frankl

text: Those who have a 'why' to live, can bear with almost any 'how'.
author: Viktor Frankl

text: Talent hits a target no one else can hit; genius hits a target no one else can see.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer

text: The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: As a tale, so is life: not how long it is, but how good it is, is what matters.
author: Seneca

text: No man was ever wise by chance.
author: Seneca

text: Accept the things to which fate binds you, and love the people with whom fate brings you together, but do so with all your heart.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: The most manifest sign of wisdom is a continual cheerfulness.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Essays, I: On the Education of Children

text: We are all patchwork, and so shapeless and diverse in composition that each bit, each moment plays its own game.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Essays, II: On the Inconstancy of Our Actions

text: The most fruitful and natural exercise of the mind, in my opinion, is conversation; I find the use of it more sweet than of any other action of life.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Essays, III: Of the Art of Conference

text: I quote others only the better to quote myself.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: The utility of living consists not in the length of days, but in the use of time.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Essays, I: That to Study Philosophy Is to Learn to Die

text: To compose our character is our duty, not to compose books, and to win, not battles and provinces, but order and tranquility in our conduct.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: On the loftiest throne in the world, we are still sitting on our bottom.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: I speak truth, not so much as I would, but as much as I dare; and I dare a little the more, as I grow older.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: There is no desire more natural than that of knowledge.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: A well-made rather than a well-filled head.
author: Michel de Montaigne
source: Essays, I: On the Education of Children

text: My trade and art is to live.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Because it was he, because it was I.
author: Michel de Montaigne

text: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.
author: Francis Bacon

text: Virtue is like a rich stone, best plain set.
author: Francis Bacon

text: Prosperity doth best discover vice, but adversity doth best discover virtue.
author: Francis Bacon

text: Fortune is like the market; where many times if you can stay a little, the price will fall.
author: Francis Bacon

text: It is a mere and miserable solitude to want true friends; without which the world is but a wilderness.
author: Francis Bacon

text: Travel, in the younger sort, is a part of education; in the elder, a part of experience.
author: Francis Bacon

text: Nature is often hidden; sometimes overcome; seldom extinguished.
author: Francis Bacon

text: Boldness is ever blind; for it seeth not dangers and inconveniences.
author: Francis Bacon

text: Our virtues are most frequently but vices disguised.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: Self-love is the greatest of flatterers.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: Neither the sun nor death can be looked at without winking.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: We are never so happy or so unhappy as we suppose.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: The head is ever the dupe of the heart.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: Nothing is given so profusely as advice.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: We become so accustomed to disguise ourselves to others that at last we are disguised to ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: There is great ability in knowing how to conceal one's ability.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: We hardly find any persons of good sense, save those who agree with us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: Few know how to be old.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld

text: The most wasted of all days is that on which you have not laughed.
author: Nicolas Chamfort

text: Happiness is not an easy thing: it is very difficult to find it within ourselves, and impossible to find it elsewhere.
author: Nicolas Chamfort

text: Society is composed of two great classes: those who have more dinners than appetites, and those who have more appetites than dinners.
author: Nicolas Chamfort

text: A clever man would be greatly embarrassed without the company of fools.
author: Nicolas Chamfort

text: The best philosophy, as applied to this world, is to combine sarcasm with cheerfulness.
author: Nicolas Chamfort

text: There is nothing so rare as true kindness; even those who believe they possess it usually have only complacency or weakness.
author: Nicolas Chamfort

text: We should not judge a man's merit by his qualities, but by the use he makes of them.
author: Nicolas Chamfort

text: There is one thing rarer, finer, and happier than talent: the ability to recognize talent in others.
author: Nicolas Chamfort

text: Great thoughts come from the heart.
author: Marquis de Vauvenargues

text: Reason leads us astray more often than nature.
author: Marquis de Vauvenargues

text: Patience is the art of hoping.
author: Marquis de Vauvenargues

text: One cannot be just if one is not humane.
author: Marquis de Vauvenargues

text: It is easier to know mankind in general than a particular man.
author: Marquis de Vauvenargues

text: Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Insist on yourself; never imitate.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Nothing is at last sacred but the integrity of your own mind.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Society everywhere is in conspiracy against the manhood of every one of its members.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: For every thing you have missed, you have gained something else; and for every thing you gain, you lose something.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: A friend may well be reckoned the masterpiece of nature.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: The sun shines to-day also. There is more wool and flax in the fields. There are new lands, new men, new thoughts.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: Earth laughs in flowers, to see her boastful boys, earth-proud, proud of the earth which is not theirs.
author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

text: I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.
author: Henry David Thoreau
source: Walden, Where I Lived, and What I Lived For

text: Morning is when I am awake and there is a dawn in me.
author: Henry David Thoreau
source: Walden, Where I Lived, and What I Lived For

text: We must learn to reawaken and keep ourselves awake, not by mechanical aids, but by an infinite expectation of the dawn, which does not forsake us in our soundest sleep.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; that is where they should be. Now put the foundations under them.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: The cost of a thing is the amount of what I will call life which is required to be exchanged for it.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Time is but the stream I go a-fishing in.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: Could a greater miracle take place than for us to look through each other's eyes for an instant?
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: In Wildness is the preservation of the world.
author: Henry David Thoreau

text: One of the pleasantest things in the world is going a journey: but I like to go by myself.
author: William Hazlitt

text: Thought depends on the habitual exercise of the speculative faculties; action, on the determination of the will.
author: William Hazlitt

text: It asks a troublesome effort to ensure the admiration of others: it is a still greater one to be satisfied with one's own thoughts.
author: William Hazlitt

text: It is better to be able neither to read nor write than to be able to do nothing else.
author: William Hazlitt
source: Table-Talk, On the Ignorance of the Learned

text: To write a genuine familiar or truly English style is to write as any one would speak in common conversation who had a thorough command and choice of words.
author: William Hazlitt

text: Hasty compositions, however they please at first by flowery luxuriance, can seldom endure the change of seasons, but perish at the first blast of criticism, or frost of neglect.
author: Samuel Johnson

text: Wonder is a pause of reason, a sudden cessation of the mental progress.
author: Samuel Johnson

text: The first task is to search books, the next to contemplate nature.
author: Samuel Johnson

text: The disposition to defer every important design to a time of leisure, and a state of settled uniformity, proceeds generally from a false estimate of the human powers.
author: Samuel Johnson

text: Calamity will neither be repelled by fortitude, nor escaped by flight; neither awed by greatness, nor eluded by obscurity.
author: Samuel Johnson

text: A woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
author: Virginia Woolf
source: A Room of One's Own, Ch. I

text: Fiction is like a spider's web, attached ever so lightly perhaps, but still attached to life at all four corners.
author: Virginia Woolf
source: A Room of One's Own, Ch. II

text: One cannot think well, love well, sleep well, if one has not dined well.
author: Virginia Woolf
source: A Room of One's Own, Ch. I

text: Lock up your libraries if you like; but there is no gate, no lock, no bolt that you can set upon the freedom of my mind.
author: Virginia Woolf
source: A Room of One's Own, Ch. IV

text: Life for both sexes—and I looked at them, shouldering their way along the pavement—is arduous, difficult, a perpetual struggle. It calls for gigantic courage and strength.
author: Virginia Woolf
source: A Room of One's Own, Ch. II

text: He who fights with monsters might take care lest he thereby become a monster. And when you gaze long into an abyss the abyss also gazes into you.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: For believe me! — the secret for harvesting from existence the greatest fruitfulness and the greatest enjoyment is: to live dangerously!
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: One thing is needful — to 'give style' to one's character.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: We want to be poets of our life — first of all in the smallest most everyday matters.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: How well disposed would you have to become to yourself and to life to crave nothing more fervently than this ultimate eternal confirmation and seal?
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: What does your conscience say? — 'You shall become the person you are.'
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: I mistrust all systematizers and avoid them. The will to a system is a lack of integrity.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Twilight of the Idols, 'Maxims and Arrows', §26

text: Without music, life would be a mistake.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Twilight of the Idols, 'Maxims and Arrows', §33

text: Only thoughts reached by walking have value.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Twilight of the Idols, 'Maxims and Arrows', §34

text: I teach you the Overman. Man is something which shall be surpassed.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: What is great in man is that he is a bridge and not a goal.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: There is always some madness in love. But there is also always some reason in madness.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Part 1, 'On Reading and Writing'

text: It is true: we love life not because we are used to living, but because we are used to loving.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Part 1, 'On Reading and Writing'

text: It is the stillest words that bring on the storm. Thoughts that come on doves' feet guide the world.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Part 2, 'The Stillest Hour'

text: It is out of the deepest depth that the highest must come to its height.
author: Friedrich Nietzsche

text: Every man takes the limits of his own field of vision for the limits of the world.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer

text: The two foes of human happiness are pain and boredom.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Aphorisms on the Wisdom of Life, ch. 2 'What a Man Is'

text: Reading is thinking with some one else's head instead of one's own.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Parerga and Paralipomena, Vol. 2, ch. 22 'On Thinking for Yourself'

text: Buying books would be a good thing if one could also buy the time to read them in: but as a rule the purchase of books is mistaken for the appropriation of their contents.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Parerga and Paralipomena, Vol. 2, ch. 23 'On Books and Reading', §296a

text: Each day is a little life: every waking and rising a little birth, every fresh morning a little youth, every going to rest and sleep a little death.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Parerga and Paralipomena, Vol. 2, ch. 2 'Our Relation to Ourselves'

text: The discovery of truth is prevented more effectively, not by the false appearance things present and which mislead into error, not directly by weakness of the reasoning powers, but by preconceived opinion, by prejudice.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer

text: Wealth is like sea-water; the more we drink, the thirstier we become.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
source: Parerga and Paralipomena, Vol. 1 (E. F. J. Payne trans., p. 347)

text: Noise is the most impertinent of all forms of interruption. It is not only an interruption, but also a disruption of thought.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer

text: There is but one truly serious philosophical problem and that is suicide. Judging whether life is or is not worth living amounts to answering the fundamental question of philosophy.
author: Albert Camus

text: We get into the habit of living before acquiring the habit of thinking.
author: Albert Camus

text: The preceding merely defines a way of thinking. But the point is to live.
author: Albert Camus

text: There is no fate that can not be surmounted by scorn.
author: Albert Camus

text: The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy.
author: Albert Camus

text: His fate belongs to him. His rock is his thing.
author: Albert Camus

text: The absurd man says yes and his effort will henceforth be unceasing.
author: Albert Camus

text: There is merely bad luck in not being loved; there is misfortune in not loving.
author: Albert Camus

text: Man first of all exists, encounters himself, surges up in the world — and defines himself afterwards.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: Man is nothing else but that which he makes of himself. That is the first principle of existentialism.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: Man is nothing else but what he purposes, he exists only in so far as he realizes himself, he is therefore nothing else but the sum of his actions, nothing else but what his life is.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: Existence precedes and rules essence.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: Man is a useless passion.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: We will freedom for freedom's sake, in and through particular circumstances. And in thus willing freedom, we discover that it depends entirely upon the freedom of others and that the freedom of others depends upon our own.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: Our responsibility is much greater than we might have supposed, because it involves all mankind.
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: Quietism is the attitude of people who say, "let others do what I cannot do."
author: Jean-Paul Sartre

text: How absurd men are! They never use the liberties they have, they demand those they do not have. They have freedom of thought, they demand freedom of speech.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: Marry, and you will regret it. Do not marry, and you will also regret it. Marry or do not marry, you will regret it either way.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: Most men pursue pleasure with such breathless haste that they hurry past it.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: Let others complain that the age is wicked; my complaint is that it is paltry; for it lacks passion.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: One must learn to know oneself before knowing anything else. Not until a person has inwardly understood himself and then sees the course he is to take does his life gain peace and meaning.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: The thing is to find a truth which is true for me, to find the idea for which I can live and die.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: What is a poet? An unhappy man who conceals profound anguish in his heart, but whose lips are so fashioned that when sighs and groans pass over them they sound like beautiful music.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: Old age realizes the dreams of youth: look at Dean Swift; in his youth he built an asylum for the insane, in his old age he was himself an inmate.
author: Søren Kierkegaard

text: Let us cultivate our garden.
author: Voltaire

text: Work then without disputing; it is the only way to render life supportable.
author: Voltaire

text: Our labor keeps off from us three great evils — idleness, vice, and want.
author: Voltaire

text: Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is an absurd one.
author: Voltaire
source: Letter to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia (28 November 1770)

text: The best is the enemy of the good.
author: Voltaire

text: Dear friend, all theory is gray, And green the golden tree of life.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The deed is everything, the glory nothing.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Of freedom and of life he only is deserving Who every day must conquer them anew.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Nothing should be treasured more highly than the value of the day.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: You really only know when you know little. Doubt grows with knowledge.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
author: Simone de Beauvoir

text: Freedom is the source from which all significations and all values spring.
author: Simone de Beauvoir

text: To will oneself free is also to will others free.
author: Simone de Beauvoir

text: Man can find a justification of his own existence only in the existence of other men.
author: Simone de Beauvoir

text: It is doubtless impossible to approach any human problems with a mind free from bias.
author: Simone de Beauvoir

text: Men, though they must die, are not born in order to die but in order to begin.
author: Hannah Arendt

text: The miracle that saves the world, the realm of human affairs, from its normal, "natural" ruin is ultimately the fact of natality, in which the faculty of action is ontologically rooted. It is, in other words, the birth of new men and the new beginning, the action they are capable of by virtue of being born.
author: Hannah Arendt

text: Man cannot be free if he does not know that he is subject to necessity, because his freedom is always won in his never wholly successful attempts to liberate himself from necessity.
author: Hannah Arendt

text: It is, in fact, far easier to act under conditions of tyranny than it is to think.
author: Hannah Arendt

text: It was indeed their search for "true reality" that led them to lose confidence in appearances, in the phenomena as they reveal themselves of their own accord to human sense and reason.
author: Hannah Arendt
source: Between Past and Future, 'The Conquest of Space and the Stature of Man'

text: Action is the pointer which shows the balance. We must not touch the pointer but the weight.
author: Simone Weil

text: Imaginary evil is romantic and varied; real evil is gloomy, monotonous, barren, boring. Imaginary good is boring; real good is always new, marvelous, intoxicating.
author: Simone Weil

text: We believe we are rising because while keeping the same base inclinations (for instance: the desire to triumph over others) we have given them a noble object. We should, on the contrary, rise by attaching noble inclinations to lowly objects.
author: Simone Weil

text: Perfection is impossible without humility. Why should I strive for perfection, if I am already good enough?
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: One hour of honest, serious thinking is more precious than weeks spent in empty talk.
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: Do not fear the lack of knowledge, fear false knowledge.
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: A pleasure to last a lifetime.
author: Charles Darwin

text: A false or inaccurate fact does essential injury, for it endures a long time; but a true fact, even if for some time unproven, may do great good.
author: Charles Darwin

text: If I had been obliged to graduate from simply observing and collecting results, I could not have written down the Origin.
author: Charles Darwin

text: The love of all things of nature is indeed a most important element in the character of a naturalist.
author: Charles Darwin

text: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species, 1st ed. 1859, concluding paragraph

text: Natural selection is daily and hourly scrutinising, throughout the world, every variation, even the slightest; rejecting that that is bad, preserving and adding up all that is good; silently and insensibly working, whenever and wherever opportunity offers, at the improvement of each organic being.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species, 1st ed. 1859, Chapter IV

text: If it could be demonstrated that any complex organ existed, which could not possibly have been formed by numerous, successive, slight modifications, my theory would absolutely break down.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species, 1st ed. 1859, Chapter VI

text: Nature may be compared to a surface covered with ten thousand sharp wedges, packed close together and driven inwards by incessant blows.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species, 1st ed. 1859, Chapter IV

text: I have steadily endeavoured to keep my mind free so as to give up any hypothesis, however much beloved (and I cannot resist forming one on every subject), as soon as the facts are shown to be opposed to it.
author: Charles Darwin

text: One never notices what has been done; one can only see what remains to be done.
author: Marie Curie
source: Letter to her brother Józef Skłodowski, 1894 (in Ève Curie, Madame Curie, 1937)

text: We must have perseverance and, above all, confidence in ourselves. We must believe that we are gifted for something and that this thing must be attained.
author: Marie Curie
source: Letter to her daughters, 1910s; widely reproduced in Ève Curie, Madame Curie (1937)

text: I am among those who think that science has great beauty.
author: Marie Curie
source: Nobel Prize banquet address, Stockholm, December 1911 (as reported in contemporary accounts and Ève Curie, Madame Curie)

text: It is the very spirit of science that makes the work of the scientist beautiful and almost joyous.
author: Marie Curie
source: Autobiographical notes appended to Pierre Curie (Paris, 1923)

text: In science, we must be interested in things, not in persons.
author: Marie Curie
source: Attributed to Curie's writings on scientific ethics (1920s); attestation moderate — see ledger

text: What I cannot create, I do not understand.
author: Richard Feynman
source: Blackboard note written at his death, February 1988 (feynmanlectures.caltech.edu photographs; Caltech Archives)

text: Nature uses only the longest threads to weave her patterns, so that each small piece of her fabric reveals the organization of the entire tapestry.
author: Richard Feynman
source: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I (1963), Ch. 2

text: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.
author: Richard Feynman
source: Caltech commencement address, 1974 ('Cargo Cult Science'; reprinted in Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!)

text: I would rather have questions that can't be answered than an answer which I can't question.
author: Richard Feynman
source: BBC Horizon interview 'The Pleasure of Finding Things Out', 1981

text: You can know the name of a bird in all the languages of the world, but when you're finished, you'll know absolutely nothing whatever about the bird.
author: Richard Feynman
source: 'The Pleasure of Finding Things Out' (1981 BBC interview); reprinted in The Pleasure of Finding Things Out (1999)

text: The cosmos is within us. We are made of star-stuff. We are a way for the universe to know itself.
author: Carl Sagan
source: Cosmos (1980), final chapter / TV series epilogue

text: The sky calls to us. If we do not destroy ourselves, we will one day venture to the stars.
author: Carl Sagan

text: Our posturings, our imagined self-importance, the delusion that we have some privileged position in the Universe, are challenged by this point of pale light.
author: Carl Sagan
source: Pale Blue Dot (1994), Ch. 3 'The Great Demotions'

text: Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known.
author: Carl Sagan
source: Attributed in Sharon Levy's biography of Sagan (1998); attestation moderate — see ledger

text: However difficult life may seem, there is always something you can do and succeed at.
author: Stephen Hawking
source: Statement accompanying the 2013 film 'Hawking' / widely reported speech, 2013

text: Look up at the stars and not down at your feet. Try to make sense of what you see.
author: Stephen Hawking
source: Interview on the nature of curiosity, Newsweek, 1988 (short form)

text: Chance favors the prepared mind.
author: Louis Pasteur

text: Imagination is the discovering faculty, pre-eminently.

text: The more I study, the more insatiable do I feel my genius for it to be.

text: I never am really satisfied that I understand anything; because, understand it well as I may, my comprehension can only be an infinitesimal fraction of all I want to understand.

text: Consciousness is a singular of which the plural is unknown.

text: A new scientific truth does not triumph by convincing its opponents and making them see the light, but rather because its opponents eventually die and a new generation grows up that is familiar with it.

text: Curiosity has its own reason for existing. One cannot help but be in awe when he contemplates the mysteries of eternity, of life, of the marvellous structure of reality.

text: Life is like riding a bicycle. To keep your balance you must keep moving.
author: Albert Einstein
source: Letter to his son Eduard, 5 February 1930 (Einstein Archives)

author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species (1859), ch. IV 'Natural Selection'

text: A grain in the balance will determine which individual shall live and which shall die, — which variety or species shall increase in number, and which shall decrease, or finally become extinct.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species (1859), ch. XIV 'Recapitulation'

text: My mind seems to have become a kind of machine for grinding general laws out of large collections of facts, but why this should have caused the atrophy of that part of the brain alone, on which the higher tastes depend, I cannot conceive.

text: From my early youth I have had the strongest desire to understand or explain whatever I observed, — that is, to group all facts under some general laws.

source: Autobiography (in The Life and Letters of Charles Darwin, ed. Francis Darwin, 1887)

text: Nothing is easier than to admit in words the truth of the universal struggle for life, or more difficult — at least I have found it so — than constantly to bear this conclusion in mind.
author: Charles Darwin
source: On the Origin of Species (1859), ch. III 'Struggle for Existence'

text: You cannot hope to build a better world without improving the individuals. To that end each of us must work for his own improvement, and at the same time share a general responsibility for all humanity, our particular duty being to aid those to whom we think we can be most useful.

source: 'The Value of Science' (1955), in What Do You Care What Other People Think? (1988)

text: Study hard what interests you the most in the most undisciplined, irreverent and original manner possible.

source: Letter to J. M. Szabados (30 November 1965), in Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track (2005)

text: Supposing, for instance, that the fundamental relations of pitched sounds in the science of harmony and of musical composition were susceptible of such expression and adaptations, the engine might compose elaborate and scientific pieces of music of any degree of complexity or extent.

text: I can see no other escape from this dilemma (lest our true aim be lost for ever) than that some of us should venture to embark on a synthesis of facts and theories, albeit with second-hand and incomplete knowledge of some of them — and at the risk of making fools of ourselves.

text: The difference in structure is of the same kind as that between an ordinary wallpaper in which the same pattern is repeated again and again in regular periodicity and a masterpiece of embroidery, say a Raphael tapestry, which shows no dull repetition, but an elaborate, coherent, meaningful design traced by the great master.
